meaning: She who works from afar (from ἑκάς)

phonemes.desc: Rough breathing on short epsilon — the name begins with an audible exhalation, like a breath across a threshold.
Kappa plus acute on short alpha — the pitch peak, a sudden calling note.
Long eta, the final syllable that draws the name into the dark.

pronunciation.approximation: 'he-KAH-tay' — the second syllable rises in pitch, and the final 'ay' is held long like the 'a' in 'say' stretched out.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: ἑκάς (hekas), 'far' — the traditional etymology, making her 'the far-working one'

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: *seh₂k- or *wekʷ-, speculative; Beekes argues for Pre-Greek origin

kin.label: Later cult
kin.form: Hekatē as torch-bearing goddess at crossroads and in the underworld

pronunciation.note: Hekátē is dual-tier because the Greek Ἑκάτη carries both stress (acute on alpha) and length (eta in the final syllable), and because two historically defensible restorations exist: Hekátē with acute stress and Hekatē with macron-only length. The form is etymologically debated, but both Unicode forms are orthographically legitimate.

domains.title: The Torch-Bearer at the Crossroads
domains.subtitle: Magic, Crossroads, Ghosts, and the Moon
domains.lead: Hekátē is the most liminal of the Greek gods. She stands at crossroads, doorways, and the boundary between living and dead. Unlike the Olympians who shine in public cult, she belongs to night, household ritual, and secret knowledge.

cards.name: The Three Ways
cards.desc: Crossroads (trioditis) are her sacred places; offerings were left at three-way intersections.

cards.name: Torch and Flame
cards.desc: She carries torches to guide Persephonē from the underworld and to light nocturnal rites.

cards.name: Ghosts and the Dead
cards.desc: She rules phantoms and sends nightmares; her bark brings the dead.

cards.name: Magic and Witchcraft
cards.desc: Patron of pharmakeia and binding spells; Medea and Circe invoke her power.

symbols.name: Twin torches
symbols.meaning: Light in darkness and the guide between worlds

symbols.name: Key
symbols.meaning: She holds the keys to the underworld and to locked mysteries

symbols.name: Dagger
symbols.meaning: Used in magical rites and as protector of doorways

symbols.name: Black dog
symbols.meaning: The Hecatean hound, associated with her nocturnal processions

symbols.name: Pole-star
symbols.meaning: Her celestial guide for sailors and night-travelers

symbols.name: Mandrake and aconite
symbols.meaning: Poisonous plants of witchcraft under her patronage

mythology.lead: Hekátē's mythology is small in scale but vast in implication. She is a Titan who keeps her power after the fall of the Titans, and she becomes Persephonē's companion in the underworld.

myths.title: Daughter of Persês
myths.text: Hesiod (Theogony 409–452) makes Hekátē the daughter of the Titan Persês and the nymph Asteria. Zeús honors her above all other Titans, granting her a share of earth, sea, and sky. This triple portion makes her uniquely able to move between realms — a goddess of boundaries because she owns all boundaries.

myths.title: Torch-Bearer in the Dark
myths.text: When Hádês seized Persephonē, Hekátē heard her cries. Later, she becomes Persephonē's companion in the underworld, carrying torches. In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, she is the one who first suggests that Hermês descend to retrieve Persephonē — a mediator between the realms.

myths.title: Asteria Becomes the Island
myths.text: Hekátē's mother Asteria, pursued by Zeús, transformed into a quail and then into the floating island of Delos — the same island that later sheltered Apóllōn and Artemis. The myth links Hekátē's lineage to the most sacred place in the Aegean.

myths.title: The Chaldean Hekátē
myths.text: In the Chaldean Oracles and Neoplatonic theurgy, Hekátē becomes a cosmic mediatrix, a lunar intellect that channels divine power. This philosophical Hekátē influenced Renaissance magic and modern Wicca, where she remains one of the most invoked goddesses.

lore.syncretism: Hekátē absorbed many minor deities of thresholds, ghosts, and night. In Roman religion she was identified with Trivia, the goddess of crossroads, and with the lunar Diana and underworld Proserpina in the famous 'triple Hecate' of later art. In Egypt she was associated with Isis and Nephthys as a goddess of magic. The Hellenistic and Roman world saw her cult spread through household rituals and curse tablets; her name appears in hundreds of magical papyri. In modern Neopaganism she is perhaps the most widely worshipped Greek goddess, embodying feminine magical autonomy.
lore.culturalLegacy: Hekátė's legacy is the persistence of magic itself. Shakespeare's witches in Macbeth invoke her by name; she appears in Goethe's Faust, in the poetry of Baudelaire, and in countless works of fantasy. The word 'hecate' became an adjective for witchcraft. Her triple form — three faces looking down three roads — is one of the most enduring images of the uncanny. Restoring Hekátē in Unicode honors not only a Greek goddess but the long, often persecuted tradition of liminal knowledge that she represents.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Hekátē is the goddess of the in-between: not day, not night; not Olympian, not chthonic; not alive, not dead. She stands at the crossroad where three paths meet and no direction is obviously right. That is why she belongs to magic: magic is the art of operating at boundaries, of making something happen by standing in the threshold.

In a culture obsessed with clarity and categories, Hekátē is unsettling because she refuses them. She is powerful precisely where definitions fail. To restore her name is to admit that the ancient world knew something we often forget: that the most important places are the ones between.
lore.archaeology: The great Carian sanctuary of Hekate at Lagina (Stratonicea) produced a Doric frieze depicting her myth and annual festival; excavations revealed the propylon and sacred way. In Athens and Selinous, inscribed lead curse tablets (defixiones) invoke Hekate for binding enemies. Marble reliefs from the Athenian Agora and Piraeus show the goddess as three-bodied Hekate Epipyrgidia or carrying torches, keys, and daggers beside crossroad pillars.
